blocks.text: The Feast with No Host
Era Three · Happy civic comedy · Five movements
I. The invitation
Tavi arrived at Doorway Plaza carrying a soup tureen larger than their head and a notice saying that everybody had already agreed.

This was an error. Everybody had agreed that somebody ought to organize a meal. Brindle, who had written the notice, considered the distinction an obstacle deliberately introduced by people who did not want to wash bowls.

The old doorway shaded six streets. Its upper hinge was a garden; its lower hinge contained a bathhouse, a repair stall, and a neighborhood argument about whether the bathhouse had been there first. The room beyond the doorway had remained asleep for longer than anyone could count. Sometimes the threshold emitted a pale pulse, and merchants lifted their goods off the ground until it passed.
Tavi delivered things between the streets. They had four carrying arms and two excellent climbing feet, which had encouraged the plaza to believe that Tavi also possessed unlimited time.
“It says I'm hosting,” Tavi told Brindle.
“You have the soup.”
“I'm taking this to Eme.”
“An excellent beginning.”

Eme lived above the bathhouse and had recently exchanged a long-legged traveling body for a broad, low form better suited to the joints that still hurt in damp weather. Their old table now stood at forehead height. Tavi was bringing supper until the carpenters finished arguing about whether shortening a table counted as destroying it.
The soup smelled of toasted grain and sour leaves. It had already escaped through one corner of its lid.
“Somebody has to begin,” Brindle said.
Brindle's own body was mostly shell. When embarrassed, they withdrew everything except their voice, and continued being unreasonable from safety.
Tavi took the service stair behind the bathhouse. Where the stair should have turned, a small amber door stood open.
They had passed that wall every day for three years.

Beyond it were counters at several heights, warm surfaces, clean water, and bowls that did not match. A narrow window shone onto no visible street. The tureen stopped leaking when Tavi set it down, chiefly because the counter was level.
There was no welcoming voice. A cloth moved along the opposite worktop on a little cleaning track, pushed a grain into a drain, and stopped.
Tavi reheated Eme's soup. Then they washed the tureen's outside, found a low tray, and laughed with the relief of someone who had been carrying too much.
II. The distinguished guests
By the next morning Brindle knew about the kitchen.
This was because Tavi had told Eme, and Eme had told Brindle while asking whether a person could reasonably shorten a chair without convening a history council.
Brindle appeared with a banner: THE FIRST GREAT FEAST OF DOORWAY PLAZA.
“Not the first,” Eme said. “I attended three before you hatched.”
Brindle turned the banner over. There was room on the back.
They went to inspect the kitchen, carrying the banner, a ceremonial ladle, and a list of distinguished guests. They found a wall.
Tavi arrived with a bowl of porridge for Eme. The amber door opened.

For a while they tested the matter badly. Brindle carried an empty bowl. Wall. Brindle carried a bowl containing their own lunch. Wall. Brindle announced that their lunch was now a diplomatic gift to the public. Wall.
“Perhaps,” Eme said, “the public can eat your announcement.”
Brindle went quiet inside the shell.
Later a young neighbor brought sliced fruit for a sibling who was repairing the hinge garden. The doorway appeared. Tavi did not see Brindle watch this, or see them put away the ceremonial ladle.
At noon Brindle returned with a small pot of grain softened exactly as Eme liked it. No banner. No audience.
The door opened.
“I used the wrong sour leaf,” Brindle said.
“I know,” said Eme, tasting it. “Sit down.”
They did.

The kitchen became crowded by accident. People arrived carrying food for friends, then stayed to prepare the next meal. Someone mended a handle. Someone else adjusted a stool. A neighbor who could not tolerate the grain's steam worked beside the cool counter, folding bright strips of leaf around crisp seeds.
Nobody discovered a control for unlimited food. Supplies still had to be grown, traded, fetched, and washed. Tavi established this firmly after the third visitor asked the cupboards for a cake.
III. Reservations
The kitchen could prepare a feast, but it could not seat one. Even Brindle admitted that thirty-seven guests, eleven companion creatures, and a band would make it difficult to reach the sink.
Eme suggested the Unclaimed Balcony.

It stood between the bathhouse and the old route office. Each building insisted that the other owned it. The balcony consequently enjoyed a view wider than the space between the buildings, two kinds of railing, and no rent collector.
Eme remembered eating there long ago.
“Was the meal good?” Tavi asked.
“My companion was. I have forgotten the meal.”
Brindle reserved it immediately.
On the evening of the feast, the entrance vanished.
The guests stood on the landing holding warm dishes. Beyond Tavi's shoulder, the band practiced a chord which had not improved during practice.
Brindle showed the wall their reservation.
The wall remained unimpressed.

The bathhouse keeper emerged, explaining that the route office had approved the exclusive booking. The route clerk emerged, explaining that the bathhouse had accepted responsibility. Each produced a copy of Brindle's form.
“You said nobody owned it,” Brindle whispered.
“Nobody did,” said Eme.
The clerk looked at the forms, the wall, and the twelve trays waiting behind it. They were hungry enough to understand very quickly.
They withdrew the booking. The bathhouse keeper withdrew their acceptance. The entrance returned between two damp pots of climbing vine.
Brindle reached for a sign reading BRINDLE'S FEAST.
Tavi caught their wrist.
“For finding the place,” Brindle said weakly.
“Eme found the place.”
“For organizing.”
“You organized the wall.”
Even Brindle laughed. It came out of the shell in three small, unwilling squeaks.
IV. The table
The balcony's table was much too high for Eme.

This produced a silence worse than the wall. Tavi had remembered Eme's preferred food, Eme's bowl, even the cloth that kept the tray from sliding. They had forgotten the reason they had been delivering supper at all.
“We can lift you,” somebody offered.
Eme looked at the empty space beneath the table. “Or you can eat with me.”

The band put down its instruments. Neighbors fetched boxes, planks, little stands, a hanging tray for a guest who rested from the railing, and a wide shallow dish that could be reached from the floor. They spread the feast across several levels. Two guests chose a quieter corner. The amphibious visitors brought a basin rather than apologizing for needing one.
Tavi moved through the crowd with all four arms full. Every time they reached a seat, another bowl needed carrying.
Brindle noticed.
“This is ridiculous,” they announced.

Tavi expected a speech. Instead, Brindle tipped the ceremonial ladle into the washing tub and began washing ordinary bowls. Their shell scraped the counter. Water splashed their face. They looked furious with happiness.
A route-office clerk took over serving. The bathhouse keeper found clean cloths. Eme made room beside them.
At last Tavi sat.
The soup had cooled. They liked it better that way.

Below the balcony, a maintenance pulse passed through the plaza. Merchants lifted baskets and lowered them again. Above, someone in the hinge garden shook a cloth, releasing tiny dry petals that drifted down among the dishes.
Brindle had prepared a toast about the greatness of the occasion. When they rose, everybody groaned affectionately.
“I know,” they said. “I'll be brief.”

They thanked the growers. They thanked the carriers. They thanked the neighbors who had brought food for bodies unlike their own. They nearly thanked the kitchen for choosing them, remembered the moving cleaning cloth, and thanked whoever kept the old water line working.
Then Eme asked for another helping, and the feast continued.
V. The next morning
The story told afterward was that Tavi had tricked two officials into giving away a palace.

The route clerk disliked this version. They had voluntarily withdrawn a form, and the balcony was smaller than their office. Brindle disliked it because the story omitted their banner. Eme liked it because no one in that version tried to lift them into a chair.
Tavi did not care which version traveled. They cared that the kitchen had no food left, and that three neighbors had already volunteered to carry grain from the morning market.
They found Brindle on the service stair with a new notice.
MEALS FOR ONE ANOTHER, it read.
Below that, in smaller writing: PLEASE INCLUDE THE PEOPLE WHO CARRY THEM.

There was no founder's name. There were places for names beside growing, cooking, delivery, washing, and resting. Brindle had put their own beside washing, crossed it out, and written washing and learning not to interfere.

Eme came down on their own feet. The shortened table was ready at home. They had brought a dish for the two carpenters, who were no longer speaking to each other but had agreed, somehow, on the height.
The kitchen opened.
Tavi held the door while everyone went in. Then Brindle took the dish from their hands and held the door for them.
For once, Tavi entered carrying nothing.
